evidence_quotes.quote: Based on a multi-level perspective in transition studies, this study explores the major interplay between actors in the urban water regime and analyzes how that influences access to water among the urban poor.

In January 2011, I conducted two weeks of intensive fieldwork in disadvantaged urban areas of Hyderabad and carried out 15 in-depth interviews with residents of the three slum areas of Jagadgirigutta in Quthbullahpur, Fathenagar in Kukatpall, and Secunderabad Division in Begumpet towns.

The data analysis was based on information about water connectivity, sufficiency of supply, water filtering devices, water pressure, frequency of water availability, and affordability of price, as well as the incidence of water-related diseases and predicaments in the household.

Although these initiatives have increased the ability of users to interact with the HMWSSB effectively, they are too focused on registered consumers (Joshi 2007). This excludes the urban poor in slum areas who are neither recorded consumers nor are served by providers.

Secondly, in low-income areas the water connection is often shared among a group of households, making the water bills much higher than single household usage since the calculation is made on the basis of increasing block tariff (HMWSSB 2008).

criterion_notes.c1: Yes. Examines urban household and slum-dweller access to piped water supply services in Hyderabad, India, including network connectivity, intermittent supply, reliance on tankers/vendors, and affordability.
criterion_notes.c2: Yes under both readings. Plain wording: Examines legal, administrative, institutional, and governance arrangements in Hyderabad's urban water sector (the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act decentralization, National Water Policy, HMWSSB organizational reforms, and donor-driven cost-recovery/PPP policies). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Although framed within a macro Multi-Level Perspective (landscape-regime-niche) transition analysis, the paper explicitly analyzes concrete rule-type mechanisms governing household access and affordability: (1) tariff and cost-recovery rules, specifically increasing block tariffs (IBT) calculated per connection that push low-income households sharing a connection into unsubsidized upper blocks, metered-connection requirements that exclude poor households from 70-80% of subsidies, and full-cost recovery tariff hikes; (2) administrative connection-application and customer-service mechanisms (Single Window Cell for new water/sewer connection applications and Metro Customer Care) whose focus on registered consumers excludes unrecorded slum dwellers; and (3) utility regulatory/governance structure (semiautonomous HMWSSB board, 74th CAA municipal delegation, and withdrawal of the 50% Neeru-Meeru rainwater-harvesting subsidy).
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Qualitative empirical case study combining primary fieldwork in January 2011 (15 structured open-ended in-depth interviews, narrative walks, and in situ observation across three Hyderabad slum areas), primary document analysis (water policies, municipal City Development Plans, memoranda, and minutes of meetings), and triangulation with secondary household surveys (Raghavendra 2006, n=550; Davis et al. 2008, n=919). Primary interview findings are synthesized narratively rather than reported as standalone quantitative estimates, which remains eligible for qualitative mechanism synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: Yes. Reports outcomes on household water connectivity/coverage (95% citywide, 90% in slums, ~40% working meters), supply continuity/reliability (a few hours on alternate days in low-income areas), affordability/pricing (higher per-kiloliter charges under increasing block tariffs for shared connections, 2 to 20 times higher unit prices from tankers/vendors, and ~4% vs 0.7% income share spent on water), and exclusion of unregistered slum households from utility reforms and subsidies.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Population and unit of analysis (urban and slum households in Hyderabad, alongside city/utility regime institutions HMWSSB and GHMC), exposure (urban water governance reforms and tariff/administrative rules), outcome (household water connection, continuity, affordability, and exclusion), and study design (qualitative empirical case study using MLP triangulation) are all identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English.

study_design: Qualitative empirical case study (Multi-Level Perspective analysis triangulating primary structured open-ended interviews, narrative walks, in situ observation, document analysis, and secondary survey data)
population_and_sample: Urban residents and low-income/slum households in Hyderabad, Andhra Pradesh, India (primary qualitative sample of 15 residents interviewed across three slum areas—Jagadgirigutta, Fathenagar, and Secunderabad Division—triangulated with policy/municipal documents and secondary Hyderabad household surveys of n=550 and n=919 households; regime-level institutions HMWSSB and GHMC).
exposure: Urban water governance arrangements and rule-type utility/tariff mechanisms in Hyderabad: 74th Constitutional Amendment Act decentralization, HMWSSB semiautonomous reforms (Single Window Cell connection-application system, Metro Customer Care, Citizen's Charter focused on registered consumers), increasing block tariff (IBT) and metered-connection subsidy rules, full-cost recovery policies, and withdrawal of rainwater-harvesting subsidies.
outcome: Household water service access, network connectivity, intermittency/continuity of supply (hours on alternate days), water affordability and unit price paid (shared-connection block tariff burden, vendor prices, income share), and exclusion of unregistered slum dwellers.
rationale: Nastar (2014) is an empirical qualitative case study of urban water governance and household water access among the urban poor in Hyderabad, India. It satisfies all review-inclusion criteria (c1-c6): it examines household/slum piped water access, intermittency, and affordability (c1, c4); analyzes concrete rule-type mechanisms under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2—including increasing block tariff rules penalizing shared connections, metered-connection subsidy eligibility, full-cost recovery pricing, Single Window Cell/Metro Customer Care administrative reforms restricted to registered consumers, and semiautonomous utility structure (c2); and employs identifiable empirical case-study methods combining 15 primary slum-resident interviews, narrative walks, in situ observation, document analysis, and secondary household survey data (c3, c5) in English (c6). Confidence is rated medium because the overarching framing is a macro Multi-Level Perspective regime analysis and empirical findings synthesize primary fieldwork narratively alongside cited secondary studies rather than reporting standalone quantitative estimates from the 15 interviews, though qualitative studies remain eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis.
